item.title: can the song not have any repeating parts almost im worried its wrong
item.description:
9.1.26 11:27 pm
Q: can the song not have any repeating parts almost im worried its wrong
A: this can happen sometimes. given the fact that so many songs do repeat things, this actually heightens the need for, from time to time, a song that does not repeat things. This is what's deceptive sometimes about music (or any creative art), is to have a sense of 'life', the rules do need to sometimes change. it's like built into any rule that that rule must sometimes change. except the exception to that rule is of course there are some rules which never change. Spooky at first, but once you get the hang of this i think you'll start to treat music and songwriting no longer as a thing, but as a sort of live companion. On second thought now i'm thinking i shouldn't have just spoiled the surprise here. that one might be actually more fun to figure out for yourself over the course of many years of and turmoil and strife

item.description:

Q: I've started writing little tid-bits of songs that I'm fairly proud of and that I like, but whenever I try and write something that sounds different to whatever I'd normally write, the lyrics and chords tend to be too similar to your style to the point where I feel like I'm just copying what you're doing, and I stop feeling like I've written something unique. A: "the best way to stop stopping is to stop not starting to not stop". but that's beside the point; what i think i'm hearing is you want to be 'unique'. the power to do something unique is a power we all secretly have. it can be exhausting waiting for ourselves sometimes to stop worrying about what not to do, and who else not to be. it's a bit of a double-frustration, of not only "when will the fun begin" but then literally "this thing technically will not have the power to start until it is fun, by definition uniqueness is fun-fueled". so it can be a double wammy of facepalm as you wait patiently for yourself to peacefully forget to worry, and almost as if by accident begin to have fun. which actually is inevitable by the way, side note

item.title: can you explain the loudness wars
item.description:

Q: can you explain the loudness wars
A: basically if i produce a song, and you produce a song, and the listener listens to them at the same volume on their sound system, who's song sounds louder? In general, whoever has the louder song will stand out, make a bigger impression, seem to 'rock more', and crucially will be heard better in a crowded room. This is basically why, throughout the history of recorded music, songs generally sound louder and louder. To make this happen, you have to squish everything up against the maximum possible loudness, so that even if the listener doesnt touch the volume dial, the producer has made sure that the song's volume is basically maxxed out the whole way through. In more recent years this has probably calmed down, partly because people got sick of that flattened sound, but also because most modern streaming platforms automatically counteract this by evaluating how loud each song sounds and then turning the whole song up or down to compensate. So nowadays i think there is the idea that if you produce a song that sounds too loud it's gonna be automatically turned down anyway. some people say the loudness war may have peaked around 2006 no pun intended

Q: Everyday there is a growing longing in me to be creative in some shape or form. The problem is Im in my late twenties, I dont play any instruments (I have dabbled a bit with drums and the trumpet when I was younger, but nothing serious), I like to think I can sing, but Im not trained and I have commitment issues with basically anything new. It just feels like I will be old or die before I become proficient in anything and I regret not having started young like so many musicians that I admire. I suppose you have been making music for most of your life, but maybe you have some advice that could help me getting started. Thank you bill
A: i can tell you about a problem that other people have, which may help you. it's a different problem, which creators, musicians, artists, filmmakers etc have. And it affects people with the highest levels of experience, sometimes the problem is worse the higher their skill level is. so the problem goes like this: there is always a tendency to overestimate how daunting a project or task is, and worse, there is a tendency to forget how much the swift forces of 'magic' take over as soon as you get started. a wise music producer once said "always leave space for god to walk into the room". but it is so very common for people at the highest levels of experience to feel like they have to "make" the thing happen. and because there is no actual recipe for music or art, this is actually impossible to contrive. so people get trapped under this weight. If they're lucky, they'll have the good fortune to catch a hint somehow at what actually becomes possible on a leap of faith. So what i'm trying to say is: don't assume that there is some "complete" set of skills that will allow you to assuredly know exactly what to do. At the highest levels of the creative industry, PEOPLE DONT HAVE A CLUE WHAT THEY'RE SUPPOSED TO DO. and the ones who are brave enough and crazy enough to take some kind of leap of faith into it, and start making mistakes, letting crazy things happen, that's where you reap all the rewards, but it is particularly common for people to get more and more deeply stuck on this the more 'experience' they think they have, because they feel like they logically should know all the answers by now. but this is the great prank of the music gods. no one shall know all the answers. A: like a warning light on your car, the songwriting vehicle has this little light on the dashboard that warns you: "ATTENTION, AS OF APPROXIMATELY 2 SECONDS AGO, YOUR MELODY GOT AHEAD OF THE WORDS. THe strongest confluence of real power seems to happen when it's just all flying together, except maybe with the words like a nano second ahead, like you get maybe 7 words with no melody at all but within nano seconds the melody swoops in for it. That's usually when i get the strongest results. HOWEVER, for variety's sake it is very important to let it happen all kinds of other different ways. including entire melodies first or entire lines of words first. Sometimes the first thing i get is actually like a whole section of melody (such as the entire main melody for 'meet me in september'). A: i can't seem to answer this in less than a million words. this is my third try. For a band, for sure, it's always been clear to me that to take full advantage of a live band you gotta ditch the click. But when you're just 1 person, and you're doing all the parts yourself, separately,.... i've always gone with the assumption that to pull this off you kinda need a click in there from the beginning, to act as like scaffolding. But something came over me recently and on a curiosity binge i started testing to see who else has used clicks over the years, and it was like this whole subject opened up that i had ALMOST thought about before, but wasnt ready to really consider, as a 1-person band. I can't believe it either, but this might be the first time i really, seriously considered what you really have to gain by staying off the click. and it became fascinating to pick out which songs and artists, especially ones from that middle time period where the click was gradually starting to catch on to everyone, (with guitar bands succumbing to it last, finally as everyone moved onto protools or whatever) it became really fun to check the ones where i was 50/50 not sure whether they would have used it. And to start really thinking about what that does for the song. It was particularly fascinating to realize, so often, for the songs that didnt use click track, i found that on some level i secretly already knew. already knew the tempo fluctuates a little in those spots. Anyway, i kept checking these songs for clicks and was basically foaming at the mouth with the desire to try going off click, but i still wasnt sure it would be possible for a 1-person band. But there was 1 album left to check, actually 2, because two seperate artists came to mind, both of whom did their first solo album entirely by themselves. one in 1995 and the other in 1970. and so, before i even checked to see if they used a click, i made a deal with myself: if i find out that BOTH of these guys, doing solo albums by themselves, were able to do it without a click, then i would officially have no excuse. i was honestly expecting they would have a click, but secretly hoping they might not. well my wish came true

Like someone will tell me my art is perfect and like, yeah, okay, i made it it's something i created from my own brain and that's valuable or whatever etc, but i'm also like, No!! item.description:
9.18.26 8:07 pm
Q: Bill something i've been thinking about a lot is how can all art be perfect *and* always have room for improvement *and* nothing be perfect *at the same time*??? Like someone will tell me my art is perfect and like, yeah, okay, i made it it's something i created from my own brain and that's valuable or whatever etc, but i'm also like, No!! That's not be true!! It can't be!!! It's literally impossible!!!! Thoughts on this please, thabks!
A: this all just comes down to a word problem. Language is fun and extremely useful, for sure, but in terms of rigid accuracy, it's never gonna hold up to the nuance of infinitely complex reality. My understanding of 'perfect' is it implies only 1 totally correct result. And the only types of assignments i can think of that could have just 1 answer are non-creative assignments. Make a totally straight line. Make perfect silence. Pitch black. Solid white. Or if the assignment is to perfectly copy an image, there is 1 correct answer which is to make exactly the same image. If the goal is to imagine something, with creativity, then you don't have this single-best-answer, you actually have infinite answers that are, actually, infinitely good. Could you still use 'perfect' somewhere in here? maybe, and words always morph and change over time, because they were never fully accurate to begin with, but for now i think 'perfect' is not even a relevant concept in the field of creativity. kind of like how the Richter scale is not useful for measuring rainfall
